opus-5.5.text:
I think there's still a lot of room, honestly, though it's gotten harder to see at first glance. A few years ago you could spot the failures immediately: mangled hands, garbled text, faces that melted into the background. A lot of that has been cleaned up, so when people look at a curated set of outputs they often conclude the problem is basically solved. I don't think it is.

When I assess quality, I look at a few different axes. One is plain fidelity, meaning whether the image looks photographic or artistically coherent at the pixel level. We've made enormous progress there. But then there's compositional correctness. If you ask for three red cups to the left of a blue bowl, with one cup tipped over, do you actually get that? Models are much better than they were, but counting, spatial relationships, and binding attributes to the right objects still break more often than you'd expect, especially as prompts get longer and more specific.

Another axis is physical and semantic plausibility. Reflections that don't match the scene, shadows going in inconsistent directions, objects intersecting in ways that couldn't happen. These are subtle, and a casual viewer may not consciously notice them, but they're often why an image feels slightly off. As the obvious artifacts disappear, these second-order errors become the frontier.

Then there's controllability, which I think matters most for people who actually use these tools creatively. A beautiful image isn't much help if it's not the image you wanted. Artists and designers want to iterate: keep this character but change the lighting, move this object, keep the style consistent across a series. Consistency and fine-grained editing are still very much open problems.

Part of what makes this tricky is measurement. Automated metrics like FID or CLIP-based scores were useful early on, but they saturate and don't line up well with what humans care about at this level of quality. So we rely heavily on human evaluation, which is expensive, noisy, and depends a lot on who you ask and what you ask them to compare. I'd say one of the biggest needs in the field is better evaluation, because you can't improve what you can't reliably measure.

So my overall view is that the headroom has shifted rather than shrunk. We're past the stage of "can it make a convincing image" and into "can it make exactly the right image, reliably, in a way a person can steer." There's a long way to go on that.

r001.rationale: It contrasts polished, curated outputs with persistent failures on specific requests, including counting, spatial relationships, and longer prompts.

r002.rationale: It discusses plausibility and controllability but does not say that world knowledge will develop alongside information-seeking use cases.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I'd say there's still a lot of room, but the nature of the room has changed. A few years ago, the gaps were obvious: hands with six fingers, garbled text, objects melting into each other. Those were failures you could spot from across the street. Most of those are largely solved now, or at least solved often enough that they're no longer the story.

What's left is more subtle and, honestly, harder. The first thing is controllability. The models can produce stunning images, but getting the exact image you have in your head is still a struggle. You end up negotiating with the model through prompts, re-rolling, and hoping. For a professional, that's not a tool, that's a slot machine. So I think a huge amount of the remaining improvement isn't about raw pixel quality at all, it's about precise, predictable control over composition, lighting, identity, and edits, especially edits that preserve everything you didn't ask to change.

The second is a kind of deeper correctness. Physical plausibility, consistent geometry, lighting that actually matches the scene, reflections that make sense, and consistency across multiple images of the same character or object. The models have learned a lot of appearance statistics, but they don't really have a world model underneath, and you can feel that when you push on anything that requires reasoning about the scene rather than just rendering it.

And the third is the aesthetic dimension, which is the hardest to measure. A lot of outputs now have a very recognizable "AI look," a sort of glossy sameness. Preference tuning tends to push everything toward a mean that people rate highly in a side-by-side, but that's not the same as range, taste, or intent. So when people ask whether image quality is saturated, I'd say the benchmarks are saturating, but the actual experience of trying to make something specific is nowhere near saturated. That gap between "looks great" and "is what I wanted" is where most of the next few years of progress will live.

r001.rationale: It contrasts stunning outputs with the difficulty of reliably getting a specific intended image, describing prompting and rerolling as a slot machine.

r002.rationale: It says deeper scene understanding and a world model are needed, but does not connect their development to information-seeking use cases.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s still a lot of room for improvement, but it depends on what you mean by quality. If you mean, can a model produce a beautiful image that looks convincing at first glance, we’re already in a pretty impressive place. But that’s different from producing exactly the image you wanted.

As you ask for more specific things—multiple objects with particular relationships, a particular pose, or a small change that leaves everything else intact—you start to see the limitations. An image can look great and still fail to follow an important part of the prompt.

So I wouldn’t measure progress only by how good the best examples look. I’d also ask how reliably you can get the result you’re looking for, and how much control you have over it. There’s a lot of room to make these models more useful along those dimensions.

r001.rationale: It says models can already produce beautiful, convincing images, but struggle to reliably follow specific prompts and preserve details.

r002.rationale: It discusses prompt-following and control, but does not mention world knowledge developing alongside information-seeking use cases.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s still a lot of room for improvement, although it depends on what we mean by quality. If you look at a single image, these models can produce something that’s visually striking and very convincing. But that’s different from reliably producing the image you actually wanted.

Once you ask for specific relationships between objects, a particular number of things, or several constraints at the same time, you start to see the limitations. And for someone using these models as a creative tool, control matters a lot. Can you change one part of an image while keeping everything else consistent? Can you iterate toward a very specific result?

So I wouldn’t judge progress only by how beautiful the best examples look. I’d also look at how consistently the model follows your intent and how useful it is throughout that process of making something.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts striking, convincing single images with unreliable results when requests require specific object relationships, counts, or multiple constraints.

r002.rationale: The response discusses following intent and creative control, but does not say that world knowledge will develop alongside information-seeking use cases.
